en: 82. The Meaning of the Six Realms (Part 8). The Meaning of the Six Realms: An Exegesis through Fourfold Analysis. I. Opening and Closing [the Categories] II. Distinguishing Characteristics III.

Clarifying Causes First, the Explanation of Names. Regarding the "six realms," these are: hell-beings (*naraka*), animals (*tiryagyoni*), hungry ghosts (*preta*), humans (*manuṣya*), devas, and asuras;
these are the six. Regarding "hell-beings" (*naraka*), as explained in the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, it is not possible... [text ends].
Because it is devoid of pleasure, it is called "hell" (naraka).
In the *Dichi* (Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā),
it is explained that it is named "niraya" because it is supremely loathsome.
*Niraya* is a term from the Hu language;
here it is translated as "hell. It is a state of suffering that is unpleasant and loathsome.
The meaning is the same in both cases.
These two explanations both highlight the faults [of such views] in contrast to the mind of revulsion.
This is not merely an explanation of its name and meaning based on conventional characteristics;
if one explains it correctly,
that which is called "hell" (naraka) is as follows:
This is a name based on location.
The subterranean prisons are their place of birth.
Therefore, it is called "hell.
As for what is called "animal" (*tiryagyoni*),
it is as explained in the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*.
They are called "animals" (tiryag-yoni) because they move horizontally;
this explains their characteristics,
not the etymological meaning of the term.
If one were to provide a formal explanation:
the term "animal" (tiryagyoni) is so named because they are raised and nurtured by a master.
All people of the world may either be devoured by them or be made to serve as their laborers.
They accumulate [rebirth] in this life;
their conduct follows this principle,
and for this reason they are called "beasts" (tiryag-yoni).
Regarding those called *preta* (hungry ghosts),
as explained in the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-vyākhyā*,
they are so named because they seek [sustenance] from others.
Furthermore, they are called "hungry" because they are constantly famished and empty;
they are called "ghosts" (preta) because they are timid and full of fear.
As for those called "humans":
As explained in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā*:
because the mind is tranquil,
one is called a "human being."
This explains the person by way of their virtues.
Because a person can contemplate and sever erroneous thoughts,
it is called "tranquility of mind."
If one relies on *nirvāṇa*,
one is called a "human" because of the great debt of gratitude owed to it;
among humans, fathers, sons, and kinsmen cherish one another.
The name [of this heaven] signifies "abundant benefit.
As for what is called "heaven" (deva),
it is as explained in the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*.
Because they possess radiance,
they are called "devas" (heavenly beings).
This is an explanation based on their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, it is said that they are called "devas" because they are pure;
thus, their celestial retribution is pure.
Therefore, it is called "Pure.
According to the *Dìchí* (Yogācārabhūmi),
because that which is received is spontaneous, it is called "Heaven" (*deva*).
Asura is a foreign term; here it is called "inferior deva."
Furthermore, people traditionally transmit that his name is Asura; "a" means "non-" and "sura" means "wine."
It is not known for what reason they are called "Non-Wine Deities.
These six kinds of sūtras are called "destinies" (gati) and are also called "paths" (mārga).
As for what is called "destiny" (gati),
it is a name for the fruit given in contrast to its cause;
for the cause is that which can lead toward the fruit.
Because the fruit is the destination of the cause,
it is called a "destination" (gati).
As for that which is called the "path" (mārga):
It is named after its cause.
Both wholesome and unwholesome karma lead a person to their respective fruits.
This is what is called the Path.
The retributions of the hells and so forth are the destinations reached by that Path.
Therefore, it is called the "path" (*mārga*).
Thus, the *Bhūmivastu* states:
"Because one travels by means of unwholesome conduct, it is called an 'unwholesome path' (*akṣaṇamārga*)."
"May also be called 'paths' (mārga)" refers to their characteristics and names.
Because the six destinies are distinguished as paths, they are called the "six paths. This concludes this section.
Next, the distinctions between expansion and contraction are examined. These are not fixed;
in summary, there is only the single category of birth-and-death through segmented portions (*paricchinna-bhava*).
Alternatively, they are divided into two:
first, the evil realms;
second, the auspicious realms.
These two gates encompass [all phenomena] exhaustively.
Alternatively, they may be divided into three,
namely the fruits of birth and death within the three realms.
Alternatively, they are divided into five:
namely, the three evil realms, the devas, and humans.
For what reason are asuras not mentioned?
Recite the sutras according to the Dharma.
There are two types of asuras:
first, ghosts; second, animals.
Since they are subsumed within the two realms of ghosts and animals,
they are not discussed separately.
This is according to the Gāthā Sūtra.
There are three types of asuras:
first, animals; second, ghosts; and third, devas.
This is because they are subsumed within the three realms of existence—ghosts, animals, and devas.
They are not discussed separately;
alternatively, they may be divided into six,
as explained above.
Although asuras are subsumed under the categories of ghosts and animals,
they are divided separately because their species are so numerous.
The discourses on the variations of forms are immeasurable in their distinctions;
such are the opening and closing of these two gates. Thus ends this section.
Next, their characteristics are distinguished.
First, the hells are distinguished.
There are two types of hells.
First, the primary hells; second, the peripheral hells.
As for the primary hells, they are located beneath the great ocean.
There are eight coarse divisions and one hundred and thirty-six subtle locations.
As for the eight coarse divisions:
First, the Saṃjīva Hell;
second, the Kālasūtra Hell;
third, the Saṃghāta Hell.
Fourth, the Saṃjīva Hell; fifth, the Kālasūtra Hell;
sixth, the Tapana Hell.
The seven hot hells and the eighth, the Avīci hell,
are located five hundred yojanas beneath the great ocean to the south of here.
There is the realm of Yama;
Yama is a ghost who judges and distinguishes between sinners.
Five hundred yojanas below the realm of Yama lies the Reviving Hell (Saṃjīva),
as Nāgārjuna has explained.
In this hell, those who undergo punishment all engage in mutual strife and contention;
their malevolent minds burn with fierce intensity.
Grasping sharp knives in their hands,
they slaughter one another until they faint and die.
Due to the conditions of their past karma,
a cool breeze blows;
the hell-wardens then shout at them.
The sinners return to life;
they revive as soon as the sound is uttered.
Because their movement follows this principle, it is called the Reviving Hell (Saṃjīva).
Mostly due to killing living beings,
one is born therein. Below this hell is the Black Rope Hell.
All the instruments of suffering become even more intense than before;
with black iron ropes,
they stretch out all the sinners.
They cause all [connections] to be severed;
hence it is called "Black Rope.
In this hell, the tortures are numerous.
Because the affairs of the Black Rope Hell are so manifest, it is specifically named after them;
this is due to [the inhabitants'] slander of the virtuous,
their false speech, frivolous talk, double-tonguedness, and harsh abuse in previous lives.
They unjustly executed the innocent;
some served as treacherous scribes;
they were cruel, violent, and devoid of the Way.
Therefore, one is born therein.
Below this Hell of Black Ropes is the Hell of Crushing (Saṃghāta),
where all instruments of torture are even more severe than those previously described.
Within that [hell], the hell-wardens manifest themselves in various forms— tigers, wolves, lions, pigs, sheep, oxen, dogs, and all other species—
to maim and slaughter the offenders.
Alternatively, they may manifest two mountains that close together,
using iron wheels, iron nets, and all manner of instruments of torture to punish the sinners;
with these various instruments of suffering all brought together, they cruelly harm the sinners.
Therefore, it is called Saṃghāta (Crushing).
Because they killed many sentient beings in previous lives, they are born therein.
Following this Saṃghāta, next comes Raurava (Wailing).
All the instruments of suffering become even more intense than before.
There is a great iron city five hundred yojanas in extent,
with hell-wardens within it.
Some are hacked, some are flayed;
some are cut with blades, some are pierced with spears,
and some are whipped.
They may strike them with clubs, staffs, or pestles,
shattering their heads.
Or they are driven east and west;
such instances are not limited to one.
Because it causes all the sinners to cry out with loud voices, it is named the Hell of Wailing (Raurava).
This is truly because in previous lives they deceived others with false measures and scales,
adjudicated matters contrary to the Dharma,
and failed to return what was entrusted to them.
They oppress those who are lowly and inferior,
afflict those who are poor and suffering,
or destroy cities and towns.
They inflict injury and torment,
separate others from their kinsmen,
or even deceive and kill them under the guise of feigned kindness.
Because they cause others to cry out, they are born therein.
Below this Hell of Crying Out (Raurava) is the Hell of Great Crying Out (Mahāraurava),
where all instruments of torture are even more severe than those before.
Within [the hell],
the wardens may drive the sinners into houses of glowing iron.
It causes them to cry out with great screams,
and is thus named Mahāraurava (Great Screaming).
This is because in previous lives they habitually killed all creatures that dwell in holes.
Furthermore, because they were bound and imprisoned, or cast into deep pits and made to cry out loudly,
they are born therein; beneath this Crying Hell (Raurava) lies the Hot Hell.
All manner of painful matters there exceed even those previously described.
Within this hell, there are two copper cauldrons.
The first is named Nanda;
the second is Varuṇa.
[There is also] the water of boiling brine.
Surging waves rise within it;
there, the rakshasa jailers impale the various sinners and hurl them into its midst.
Some are thrown into pits of charcoal;
some are thrown into boiling ashes;
or they are [drenched] with pus and blood.
They are thus tormented by their own [karma] and are called the Heat Hells (Tapana-naraka),
because in previous lives they distressed and disturbed their parents, teachers, elders, and all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.
Because their minds are set ablaze, they are born therein.
Following this is the Great Heating Hell (Mahātapana),
where all forms of suffering become even more intense than before.
Because in previous lives they boiled sentient beings alive,
or caused them to rot while living,
or impaled them on wooden stakes.
They are born there and roasted alive.
Or, because they burned mountains, marshes, villages, Buddhist stupas, or monasteries,
or because they pushed sentient beings so that they fell into boiling water or fire, they are born therein.
Below this is the Avīci Hell,
as described in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
This hell is eighty thousand yojanas in length and breadth.
The suffering therein exceeds that of the previous seven hells and other separate locations by two thousandfold;
it is covered over by iron nets.
The fire from above penetrates below;
the fire from below penetrates above.
They intersect and pass through one another in total penetration.
When one person enters within,
their body also fills it completely;
when a second person enters, [the same occurs].
Their bodies likewise fill [the space],
and their lifespan lasts for one kalpa;
there is not even a moment’s respite from suffering.
Because in their previous lives they committed the five heinous crimes and slandered the Vaipulya sutras;
having given rise to great false views and slandered the existence of cause and effect, they severed their roots of goodness and were therefore born therein.
Those who commit the ten unwholesome karmas will all be born within these eight great hells;
what has been said thus far has merely been spoken according to their coarse characteristics.
Regarding the statement that there are one hundred and thirty-six:
each of the first eight hells has sixteen subsidiary hells;
eight of these are cold ice hells.
The eight [hot hells] are the fires of flame.
As for the eight cold hells,
they are as described by Nāgārjuna.
The first is Arbuda;
this is named "Many Holes.
It must be a mountain ridge with many hollows, and is thus called "Many Holes."
That is also acceptable.
This place freezes all the sinners;
because it causes many holes to be pierced [in their bodies], it is named "Many Holes" (Sūcī-mukha).
The second is the *pūtudvīpa* (Floating Island).
This is called "without holes";
it may be understood by comparison with the preceding [description].
These two types are named according to their characteristics;
the third is Ārāḍa.
This is the sound of suffering from cold: "a-pa-po-po.
This too is the sound of suffering from cold.
The fifth is called *hūhū*,
which is also a sound of cold;
these are the three types.
Based on its sound, it is named *ṣaḍ-utpala*;
this name means "blue lotus."
The appearance of the prison city resembles a blue lotus; therefore, it is named "Blue Lotus.
This is also acceptable.
In this place, various sinners are frozen;
those with a color like that of a blue lotus are called *utpala*,
and there are seven *padma* [hells].
This is called the red lotus (*padma*).
The two explanations for this term may be understood by analogy with the preceding.
Eighth is the great red lotus (*mahāpadma*).
This is called the Great Red Lotus.
Its meaning is the same as that of the three [lotuses] mentioned previously and subsequently;
it is named after its color.
As for the eight fires of hell:
the first is named the Pit of Charcoal;
the second is named Boiling Excrement.
The third is named Burning Forest;
the fourth is named Sword Tree;
the fifth is named Path of Blades.
Sixth is named Thorns and Spikes;
seventh is named Salty River;
eighth is named Copper Pillars.
Regarding the aforementioned eight great hells,
there are two [pools of] ice and two [pools of] blazing fire in each of the four directions— east, west, south,
and north. Thus, there are sixteen.
Each of the eight great hells has sixteen [subsidiary hells],
making one hundred twenty-eight locations in total;
including the eight great hells themselves, there are one hundred thirty-six.
As stated in the *Dharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*,
these one hundred and thirty-six locations each have distinct names and correspondingly distinct karmic fruits.
It cannot be discussed in full detail.
Such is the situation in the primary locations;
as for those in the peripheral hells:
Either within the Iron Ring Mountains,
or among other mountains,
or within the great ocean.
The various places where punishments for offenses are meted out are called the peripheral hells (*pratyanta-naraka*). Such are the hells.
Next, the animals (*tiryagyoni*) shall be explained.
As stated in the *Dharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*,
there are generally thirty-four billion species among the animals; within these,
there are differences regarding the four modes of birth and the four types of nutriment.
The variations in the fruits of karma are fully detailed in that sutra and cannot be recounted in their entirety; such is the case with animals.
Next, the hungry ghosts (preta) are explained as stated in the *Dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*.
Among the hungry ghosts, there are essentially two types of abodes.
The first is among humans;
the second is in the realm of hungry ghosts,
as stated in that sutra.
Five hundred yojanas below Jambudvīpa,
extending for thirty-six thousand yojanas in length and breadth,
is the realm of the hungry ghosts (preta).
The categories are distinct;
there are thirty-six types.
The first is the cauldron-bodied hungry ghost (*kumbhāṇḍa*).
Its form resembles a cauldron;
it lacks the features of a head, crown, eyes, ears, nose, tongue, hands, feet, and so forth,
and it dwells in the realm of hungry ghosts (preta).
At the time of birth,
it is twice the size of a human body;
thereafter, it gradually increases in growth.
It extends for a full yojana;
fierce flames fill the interior of the cauldron,
incinerating their bodies.
Afflicted by hunger, thirst, and the torment of heat,
there is no one able to save them;
their lifespan among humans is ten years.
During those days and nights,
the body in that cauldron endures for a lifespan of five hundred years,
because in a previous life it was hired to slaughter animals out of greed for wealth and profit.
Furthermore, because they received deposits from others and refused to return them,
they are born therein. Second are the needle-mouthed hungry ghosts (*sūcimukha*).
Their bodies are as large as mountains,
yet their mouths are like the eye of a needle;
they likewise dwell in the realm of hungry ghosts.
Their lifespan is equal to that of the cauldron itself;
the fires of hunger burn their bodies,
scorching and inflaming them without relief.
They shall also undergo all manner of sufferings from cold, heat, and various poisons,
because in previous lives they hired others to slaughter animals;
or there may be women whom their husbands commanded to provide offerings for śramaṇas of pure conduct.
They deceive others by saying things such as, "The Path does not exist," and for this reason they are born there.
Third are the *vāntāśana* (vomit-eating) pretas.
Fourth, the excrement-eating pretas;
fifth, the foodless pretas;
sixth, the breath-eating pretas.
Seventh are the *piśāca* who feed on food;
eighth are the *piśāca* who feed on water;
ninth are the *piśāca* who subsist on longing.
10. The ghosts that eat saliva;
11. The ghosts that eat garlands;
12. The ghosts that eat blood.
13. Flesh-eating ghosts;
14. Incense-smoke-eating ghosts;
15. Swift-moving ghosts.
16. The Ghosts Who Await an Opportunity;
17. The Ghosts of the Underworld;
18. The Ghosts with Supernatural Powers.
19. The Blazing Ghost;
20. The Ghost that Seeks an Infant’s Weakness;
21. The Ghost of Lustful Color.
Twenty-second are the ghosts dwelling on the islands of the sea;
twenty-third are the messengers who wield staves—
these are the kings of Yama.
Twenty-fourth, the ghosts that devour infants;
twenty-fifth, the ghosts that consume the vital essence of humans;
twenty-sixth, the rākṣasa ghosts.
Twenty-seventh are the ghosts who burn food in fire-pits;
twenty-eighth are the ghosts who dwell in impure alleys;
twenty-ninth are the ghosts who eat wind.
30. The fire-charcoal-eating spirits;
31. The poison-eating spirits;
32. The wilderness spirits.
33. The hungry ghosts who dwell among burial mounds and eat hot ashes and soil;
34. The hungry ghosts who dwell within trees;
35. The hungry ghosts who dwell at the crossroads.
There are thirty-six types of hungry ghosts who kill themselves;
though these ghosts are individually immeasurable,
they are subsumed within these categories.
The causes and effects of their karmic retributions therein differ from one another,
as fully described in the sūtras regarding hungry ghosts (preta).
Next, the asuras are examined.
According to the Gāthā, there are three types of asuras:
first, devas; second, ghosts; and third, animals.
In the *Dharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*,
only two types are mentioned:
those of the hungry ghosts and those of the animals.
As for the *asura* ghosts,
they are categorized among the hungry ghosts who have killed themselves;
they dwell upon Mount Viśvāmitra on the earth.
As for the asuras who dwell in the animal realm,
they reside on the side of Mount Sumeru in the north, beneath the ocean floor at four distinct levels.
It enters twenty-one thousand yojanas into the earth,
where the Rāhu Asura dwells;
the expanse of the ground there is thirteen thousand yojanas.
The city is named Ālokā;
it is eight thousand yojanas in length and breadth, being perfectly square,
and contains a hall with a thousand pillars.
Rows of jewel chambers line the city;
the ground, mountains, ponds, and all articles of pleasure are adorned with jewels throughout the city. Within that city:
There are four jewel gardens,
each one hundred yojanas in extent.
Within each garden, there are—
There are three thousand kinds of wish-fulfilling trees;
these trees are all made of pure gold,
and their spiritual essence is subtle and wondrous.
Like clouds and like shadows,
within its gardens and ponds, birds of various jewel-like colors gather and flock together in abundance.
The king dwells in this city.
Outside the city, there are thirteen separate residences,
and in each residence there are immeasurable hosts of asuras.
Rāhu Asura is the son of Siṃha;
his form is like Mount Sumeru.
They are able to transform their own bodies,
making them large or small at will; five hundred years among humans constitute one day and night for them.
Rāhu’s lifespan there is five thousand years.
He has four court ladies who are born from his mere thought.
He had twelve nayutas of celestial maidens as his retinue,
who surrounded Rāhu.
In the past, that king was a brahmin.
In a wilderness region, there was a Buddha stūpa twenty-five *li* in height.
Within it, one should paint various Buddha images,
diverse flowers and fruits,
and the adornments of groves and forests.
When he was being burned by fire,
this brahmin rescued him and enabled him to escape.
Having rescued it, he thought:
"I have rescued this stupa;
will there be merit from this?"
If there are those with merit,
may they obtain a large body.
Furthermore, among the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas)...
Because they practiced generosity extensively,
they receive this retribution.
As for the other asuras:
In past lives, one may have seen others killing living beings and have forcibly compelled them to release them; or,
for the sake of fame and profit.
Some act as envoys for a king;
others practice the ancestral law of non-killing,
not out of a heart of compassion.
Because they did not maintain pure precepts and did not perform various wholesome deeds,
they were born therein.
Twenty-one thousand yojanas further down is the abode of the Asuras known as the Valiant;
its king is named Valiant.
The people are named Mahu,
which in this language means "Bone-Neck.
The land is named Moon-Garland.
Gradually expanding, the city of the preceding stage is named *Vikrīḍita*;
it is eighty thousand yojanas in length and breadth, equal on all sides,
and its magnificent adornments surpass those of the former.
That city is situated amidst four golden mountains,
each of which is five thousand yojanas in height and breadth;
the king dwells in this city.
There is another city named Tārāmālā,
where the people dwell.
Outside the city there is a park,
measuring thirteen thousand yojanas in length and breadth;
within it, there are seven distinct gardens.
Adorned with various ornaments,
these asuras experience pleasure therein.
The valiant asura was tall and large in stature,
like two Mount Sumerus.
If one dwells within one's own realm,
the body transforms to become short and small,
yet its power and influence become even more superior.
Six hundred years for humans corresponds to one day and night there;
the lifespan of the asuras on this earth is six thousand such years.
In a past kalpa, that king plundered the property of others and made offerings to non-Buddhist practitioners who had renounced desire; therefore,
he has received this retribution.
Other beings were born there because in the past they had made offerings to non-Buddhist practitioners who were not free from desire,
as well as to those who had broken the precepts.
Twenty-one thousand yojanas further down lies the abode of the asuras known as Mālādhāra;
its king is named Mālādhāra.
The people were named Youxi (Game-Play);
the land was named Xiuna (Sona);
and the city was named Xiangpiluo (Kampila).
It measures thirteen thousand yojanas in length and breadth;
its adornments are exquisite and subtle,
surpassing those of the former by far.
The form assumed by the Asura Puṣpamāla is like three Sumeru mountains.
If one dwells within one's own realm,
manifesting a minute body,
one's power and influence increase further.
Seven hundred years for humans corresponds to one day and night for the asuras of this earth.
His lifespan was seven thousand years.
When that king passed away,
he had bestowed food and drink upon sick people who violated the precepts.
Therefore, they receive this retribution.
As for the rest of the multitude, due to various playful acts in their previous lives,
they gathered objects as food.
Because they gave [their wealth] to others without having a fundamentally pure mind,
they were born therein.
Twenty-one thousand yojanas further down lies the abode of the asuras known as Bāhupramati;
its king is named Bāha.
It is also called *pārahā*.
These are originally one name;
it is only that the phonetic expressions in human speech differ.
He is also named Vemacitra;
the subjects over whom he rules are called Sarvakṣānti.
The name of the land is Akṣobhya;
it is sixty thousand yojanas in extent.
The name of the city is Khāṇḍavī.
It was thirteen thousand yojanas in length and breadth;
its palaces of the seven treasures were as exquisite and subtle as those of the heavens.
Vemacitra was of immense stature,
as tall as four Mount Sumerus.
If they dwell in their original realm,
they manifest a minute body whose power surpasses that of the asuras of the three preceding stages.
Eight hundred years for humans corresponds to one day and night for the asuras here on this earth.
His lifespan was eight thousand years.
In his previous life, that king lacked right view;
when he saw one who upheld the precepts coming to beg from him, [he acted accordingly].
After a long time, he finally gave it to him.
Having given it, he said:
"I now give this to you."
"What merit is there?
Out of delusion, I gave you food and drink;
I gave with a mind of wrong view."
Therefore, they receive this retribution.
As for the remaining asura hosts,
in their previous lives...
For his own sake, he guarded and managed fruit trees and all manner of things that he himself did not use.
Thereafter, they bestow benefits upon others;
thus, they are born therein.
These are the various asuras.
They contend with the heavens as adversaries and engage in battle and competition with them,
as described in detail in the sutras.
It is impossible to describe the asuras in detail in this manner.
Next, the human realm is distinguished;
the types of humans are immeasurable.
There are approximately four,
namely the differences in the retributions of the people of the four continents.
These are the people of the four continents.
There are eight differences.
First, the difference in location:
to the south of Mount Sumeru, there is a sea-island.
It is named Jambudvīpa.
It is twenty-eight thousand li in length and breadth.
Human beings dwell upon it.
To the east there is a continent named Pūrvavideha,
which is twice as broad as Jambudvīpa.
Humans dwell upon it.
To the west lies a continent named Aparagoyānī.
It is twice as wide as Pūrvavideha,
and people dwell upon it.
To the north, there is an island.
It is named Uttarakuru;
it is twice as broad as Jambudvīpa,
and people dwell upon it.
Second, their physical forms differ.
Jambudvīpa in the south has a terrain that is pointed and slanted.
The human faces resemble those [of Jambudvīpa].
The continent of Pūrvavideha is shaped like a half-moon.
The human faces resemble those [of Jambudvīpa].
On the continent of Aparagoyānī,
the ground is like a full moon.
The human realm resembles it;
to the north lies Uttarakuru,
whose land is square.
Human faces resemble them;
however, their three dimensions differ in length.
This is the case for the people of Jambudvīpa.
The inhabitants of Jambudvīpa are four cubits in height;
those of Pūrvavideha are eight cubits in height.
The people of Aparagoyānī are sixteen cubits tall;
the people of Uttarakuru—
Thirty-two cubits in height;
fourth, differences in lifespan:
the people of Jambudvīpa.
The lifespan is indefinite;
at its shortest it is ten years,
and at its longest it is eighty-four thousand years.
The people of Pūrvavideha have a lifespan of two hundred and fifty years;

but because consciousness is the primary factor, it is mentioned specifically.
Question: There are three evil destinies within the desire realm;
why are they not mentioned?
The treatise states: "In the three evil realms, there is the torment of suffering that oppresses consciousness, so it finds no peace;
therefore, they are not discussed.
Furthermore, he asked:
The realm of form possesses the four dhyānas.
Within the fourth dhyāna, tranquility and bliss surpass those of the lower stages.
For what reason is it not called a station of consciousness?
The commentary itself states:
"Within the fourth dhyāna,
there is the attainment of non-conception."
Because it harms the consciousness, consciousness does not delight in dwelling there; therefore,
it is not a station of consciousness.
Furthermore, within the fourth dhyāna,
there are five Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa) through which one enters into nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, it impairs the mind and consciousness; since consciousness does not delight in remaining there,
it is not a station of consciousness.
Question: There are four formless abodes (ārūpya-dhātu).
For what reason is this so?
It is not stated that "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" constitutes a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
The treatise states:
"In neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there is the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)."
Furthermore, because the defiled mind and consciousness do not find peace therein,
it is not a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*). This concludes the meaning of the seven stations of consciousness.

This brief analysis is thus concluded. 84. The Meaning of the Eight Difficulties (End of Part 8). The meaning of the eight difficulties is explained through a fivefold classification: 1. Defining the Names; 2. Distinguishing the Characteristics; 3. Classification according to the Five Destinies; 4. Classification according to Afflictions, Karma, and Retribution; 5. Clarifying the Distinctions by Correlating with the Four Wheels. First, the explanation of the names.
Regarding the eight difficulties:
the first is hell;
the second is the animal realm.
Third, those who are hungry ghosts;
fourth, those who are blind, deaf, or mute; fifth, those with worldly wisdom and eloquence;
sixth, those who live before or after a Buddha.
Seventh, the continent of Uttarakuru;
eighth, the Heaven of Longevity.
These comprise the first three and the last one.
The names are established according to the destinies (*gati*).
Among these, the first three fully encompass the three destinies.
Therefore, it is stated directly that the difficulties of the hells, animals, and hungry ghosts constitute the eighth single difficulty;
it does not exhaust the realm of the gods.
They are distinguished by their long lifespans;
therefore, this is called the "difficulty of the Heaven of Long Life.
They are blind, deaf, mute, and dumb, yet possess worldly wisdom and eloquence.
The designation is established based on its actual nature;
it is precisely because the blind, the deaf, and those with worldly cleverness and eloquence are used as the objects of refutation that [the term applies] both before and after the Buddha.
Manifesting its name according to the time,
it is designated by the specific location of the Utsarpiṇī (Auspicious) aeon.
These eight kinds [of obstacles] can hinder the Noble Path;
therefore, they are called "difficulties. This concludes the first section.
Next, their characteristics will be explained.
These eight types [of consciousness] are so designated for four reasons.
This is why it is difficult:
first, because it is hindered by suffering;
second, because it is hindered by pleasure.
It is difficult because the three evil realms increase;
it is difficult because the four virtues are subtle.
All those in the three miserable paths are blind, deaf, and mute.
It is difficult because of the obstacle of suffering;
it is difficult because of the obstacle of the pleasures of long-lived Uttarakuru; and [it is difficult for] those who possess worldly wisdom and eloquence.
It is difficult because evil increases;
for their wrong views run counter to the Right Path.
This occurs both before and after a Buddha.
Because they are subtle, they are difficult [to perceive].
As for what is called the difficulty regarding the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals:
it refers to all three miserable realms.
Their karmic retribution and hindrances are so profound and heavy that they are unable to encounter the sages;
for this reason, it is difficult.
Question: If it were the case that the three miserable realms are so difficult that no noble ones (ārya) could be encountered there,
this would not be correct.
As stated in the Vaipulya sūtras:
there are sentient beings who are within the hells.
Encountering the Buddha’s radiance,
they followed the light to approach the Buddha;
hearing the Dharma, they attained the Way.
As Nāgārjuna said:
"Beings of the two destinies of hungry ghosts and animals hear the Buddha preach the Dharma."
There are those who have attained the Way,
as described in the "Deva Chapter" of the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
[Such is the case with] the deity Kūṣmāṇḍī.
They hear the Dharma and attain the Way,
as described in the *Tiwai jing* regarding the various dragons, ghosts, and spirits.
Hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma,
they all likewise attained the Way.
Among those in the three miserable realms, [they were also delivered].
"It does not hinder one from meeting the Sage. Why is this difficult?
He explained, saying:
The three miserable realms are places of obstruction and difficulty where one cannot attain the Way;
yet there are sentient beings who have long practiced superior causes.
Having encountered [the conditions] to fall into the three evil realms,
they now meet the Tathāgata and the great bodhisattvas through their inconceivable power for the sake of this chapter’s context.
There are those who have attained the Path,
such as Nanda and others, yet they remain entangled by the hindrances of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
One should not attain the Way;
it is by means of conditions that the Buddha enables one to enter the Noble Path.
This is also like that:
because one lacks personal power and minor auxiliary conditions such as the relics, it is possible to enter the Noble Path;
therefore, it is called "difficult."
Furthermore, among those in the three evil realms who encounter the sages and attain the Way,
most are persons of provisional status.
In order to lead those in other births to give rise to the mind of renunciation,
he demonstrates that there is something to be attained;
yet this is not the case for an actual ordinary person.
In truth, ordinary people cannot attain it;
therefore, it is called "difficult.
As for what is called the difficulty of being blind, deaf, mute, or speech-impaired:
The blind do not behold the Sage;
the deaf do not hear the Dharma;
the mute do not inquire or receive instruction.
Being unable to enter the state of sainthood constitutes a difficulty. Thus it is said to be difficult. He asked:
Being blind, deaf, or mute— all these are indeed obstacles. There are, however,
those that are not obstacles.
The commentary states:
Being born blind, being born deaf, and being born mute are included among the eight difficulties;
the others are not difficulties.
Question: All those who are blind, deaf,
or mute lack both seeing and hearing.
It is impossible to consult and receive [instruction].
Why, then, do you single out those who are blind from birth, deaf, and mute as being difficult?
The explanation says:
Were it not for being born blind, deaf, or mute,
one would first have been able to see a friend, hear the Dharma, and receive instruction; subsequently, one could rely on the stages of the path,
as these conditions do not constitute total obstructions.
Therefore, this is not difficult.
As for those of worldly wisdom and eloquence,
there are some who are sharp-witted yet harbor false attachments that are difficult to overturn.
This is why it is difficult.
As for what is called the "difficulty of before or after the Buddha," it refers to the periods before or after the Buddha.
When the Buddha-dharma does not exist,
one does not know the path out [of suffering] and has no mind to seek the holy.
This is why it is difficult.
A questioner asks:
"Does a pratyekabuddha appear in a world where there is no Buddha?"
"What difficulty is there in being before or after a Buddha?
Śāriputra replied,
"A Pratyekabuddha has long cultivated [the path] until it is fully matured."
They are able to cross over by their own power,
without depending on the instruction of a teacher;
as for other sentient beings...
Since there are no such persons [among them], it is said to be difficult for others. As for Uttarakuru:
In the northern continent of Uttarakuru, the retribution of pleasure is preeminent;
one beholds nothing but the absence of suffering.
Among its sentient beings, [there is no suffering].
The power of wisdom is weak;
one does not know how to cultivate weary detachment, contemplate faults, or seek liberation. Therefore, it is difficult.
Question: Since the pleasures of the desire-realm devas are superior to those of Uttarakuru,
why is it not difficult [to attain rebirth there]?
The commentary states:
Although the karmic reward of pleasure in the six heavens is superior,
the power of wisdom therein is even more enhanced.
Because they are capable of developing weary detachment, contemplating faults, and seeking liberation, this is not difficult for them.
Furthermore, within those heavens, there are mirror-forests and mirror-walls manifested by the Buddha.
Among them, the devas saw the evil destinies toward which they were headed in future lives;
their sorrow and anxiety became profound.
They lose their celestial pleasures as if separated by a thousand generations,
with nothing remaining.
Furthermore, when his retribution is about to end and the five signs of decay appear,
he is filled with grief and despair, having no recourse.
During these two periods,
one is able to cultivate revulsion toward the three realms of existence and seeks to attain liberation.
For this reason, it is criticized;
in the land of Uttarakuru,
such things do not exist.
This is why it is difficult [to distinguish them].
As for the gods of Long Life (Āyus-mahārāja-kāyika),
their life-span and karmic retribution are extended within the realms of form and formlessness.
The lowest limit is half an eon;
these are called the Gods of Long Life.
Within those heavens, there is tranquility and peace.
When ordinary beings are born there,
they mostly regard it as nirvana;
their attachment to it is deep and profound.
Furthermore, it is difficult because there is no Buddha-dharma upon which one can rely to seek liberation.
Question: Why is this so?
The Sūtras state that those who attain parinirvāṇa upon birth, through effort, or without effort, all attain the fruit of nirvāṇa within a long lifespan.
Why, then, is it said that a long lifespan is difficult?
The explanation is as follows:
The objector explains this by referring to ordinary persons;
those such as the "attainer of parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (antarāparinirvāyin) are actually *anāgāmins*.
Birth in the higher realms results in the attainment of cessation;

therefore, there is nothing beyond these two gates. Having concluded this section, we shall next distinguish the eight unfavorable conditions (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*) with respect to the five destinies (*pañcagati*).
The hells, hungry ghosts, and animals constitute the three lower realms;
these include those who are blind or deaf, those with worldly wisdom, those born before or after a Buddha, and those in Uttarakuru—
these being a small portion of the human realm.
However, among human beings,
this excludes those who are blind or deaf, those with worldly wisdom, those born before or after a Buddha, and those in Uttarakuru.
In the other three directions, [these conditions exist];
as for Uttarakuru, it exists only in the land of Uttarakuru.
Longevity is one such difficulty.
A small portion of the heavenly realms (*deva-gati*), because the heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are not difficult [to attain]. This concludes the three gates.
Next, they are distinguished according to afflictions (*kleśa*), karma (*karman*), and retribution (*vipāka*).

Regarding the difficulty of [attaining] a human rebirth, it is said that it is difficult for those in the hells, among hungry ghosts, among animals, and those who are blind, deaf, or mute, as well as those with long lifespans in Uttarakuru.
Among these, the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals are included under the category of being blind and deaf.
This is their retribution of suffering;
long life in Uttarakuru is their retribution of happiness;
and worldly wisdom and eloquence are likewise.
Because these are categorized as afflictions and subsumed under wrong views,
they are not included within the three categories of the period before a Buddha, the period after a Buddha, or the period of afflictions, karma, and retribution.
However, because there is no Buddha-dharma upon which to rely for seeking liberation, this makes it difficult;
thus concludes the discussion of these four gates.
Next, the remedies are distinguished by means of the four wheels.
What are the four wheels?
As stated in the *Tattvasiddhi*,
the first is dwelling in a favorable location.
That is to say, being born in a central land;
second, relying on virtuous persons,
which means encountering the era of a Buddha.
Third, they have personally made correct vows,
meaning they possess right view.
Fourth, they have planted roots of goodness in past lives.
This refers to having all faculties intact in the present life;
since these four exist only among gods and humans,
the treatise calls them the "Four Wheels of Gods and Humans."
What is called a "wheel" (cakra) is a designation based on a metaphor;
it is that which can crush the eight unfavorable conditions (aṣṭākṣaṇa).
Because it gives rise to the noble path and the untainted wheel of Dharma (anāsrava-dharmacakra),
it is called a "wheel" (cakra).
These four wheels are thus.
What is the method of cultivation?
As stated in the treatise:
first, dwell in a wholesome place.
It can overcome five obstacles:
namely, the three evil realms, long-lived beings, and Uttarakuru;
because one is born as a human or a deva and dwells in a central land.
Apart from these five,
"relying on virtuous persons" means remaining far removed from the calamities that occur before or after a Buddha's appearance.
Because one has encountered the era of a Buddha, one is freed from this hardship;
by making a right vow for oneself,
one distances oneself from the hardship of worldly cleverness and eloquence.
Because they seek with correctness, they are free from the obstacles of heterodoxy;
because they have planted roots of goodness in past lives,
they are far removed from the obstacles of blindness, deafness, and muteness.
Because they possess all the sense faculties,
they are free from those difficulties.
Such are the eight difficult conditions.
85. The Meaning of the Nine Abodes of Sentient Beings (Part 8): Regarding the meaning of the nine abodes of sentient beings as explained in the Sūtras, for what reason were they taught?
This is for the purpose of refuting the general reckonings of the non-Buddhists.
There are certain non-Buddhists who reckoned sentient beings collectively as a "self" (ātman).
They select what is good and dwell therein.
The Buddha refutes this;
therefore, he says that these nine abodes belong to sentient beings and are not my own abode.
What are they? The humans and devas of the desire realm constitute one.
The first dhyāna constitutes two;
the second dhyāna constitutes three;
the third dhyāna constitutes four.
The sphere of non-perception is the fifth;
the sphere of infinite space is the sixth;
the sphere of infinite consciousness is the seventh.
The sphere of nothingness is taken as the eighth; the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the ninth.
These nine places where sentient beings delight in dwelling are called the "abodes of sentient beings.
Question: [Why is this so?]
In the preceding discussion of the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*),
the realm of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*) and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) were not mentioned; why, then, are they now included here as abodes?
The commentary states:
Because consciousness is harmed in this place,
it is not a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
It does not extinguish sentient beings;
therefore, it is called the "abode of sentient beings. Question:
Within the three miserable realms of the desire realm there are also sentient beings.
Why, then, are they not described as abodes of sentient beings?
The explanation says:
Sentient beings alike loathe the three evil realms;
they are not places where one delights to dwell.
For this reason, they are not mentioned.
He asked again:
"Within the fourth dhyāna of the form realm,
excluding the Heaven of Non-conception, there are eight other heavens."
Sentient beings delight in dwelling there;
why, then, is it not called an abode of sentient beings?
The *Samyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* explains:
Within those four dhyānas,
there are five Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa),
where beings joyfully seek nirvāṇa.
They do not wish to dwell there for long;

therefore, these are not described as abodes for sentient beings. The others—the Heaven of Merit-Born (*Puṇyaprasava*), the Heaven of Merit-Love (*Vṛhatphala*), and the Heaven of Vast Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*)—are likewise [not so described].
Some seek the Pure Abodes;
some seek the Formless Realm; some seek Nirvana.
Because they do not wish to dwell there for long,
it is therefore also not an abode of sentient beings.
This is the meaning of the nine abodes.

A brief exposition concludes thus. 86. The Meaning of the Twelve Bases (*āyatana*). (End of Part 8) The Meaning of the Twelve Bases is explained through an analysis in six sections: 1. Definition of Terms; 2. Determination of Essential Nature (*svabhāva*); 3. Analysis of Characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); 4. Classification according to Meaning; 5. Classification in Relation to the Aggregates (*skandha*); 6. Classification in Relation to the Elements (*dhātu*). First: Definition of Terms.
The twelve bases (āyatana) are so called because they are the places where consciousness arises;
thus they are named "bases."
Just as the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) are called the eight spheres of removal (*abhibhāyatana*),
so too the mutual conformity and entry between the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) are also termed "entry" (*āyatana*).
The meanings of these entries differ;
when divided, they become twelve:
namely, eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, form, sound, odor, taste, tangible object, and mental phenomena.
Among these twelve,
the first six are internal and the latter six are external.
The internal are called the six sense faculties;
the external are called the six sense objects.
What is meant by "eye"?
This continues up to the term "mind" (*manas*).
There are two interpretations for this:
first, it is discussed in terms of its correspondence.
The pair consisting of visible forms is called the eye,
and so on up to the sixth pair, which consists of mental phenomena and is called the mind.
This is explained according to their functional capacity.
That which is able to see is called the eye;
that which is able to hear is called the ear;
that which is able to smell is termed the nose.
That which is capable of tasting is called the tongue;
that which is capable of sensation is termed the body;
that which is capable of thinking is called the mind.
What are name-and-form, up to and including mental phenomena (*dharma*)?
The explanation states that there are two [types].
First, it is explained by way of pairing:
that which is paired with the eye is called "form" (rūpa),
and so on, up to the sixth, which is paired with the mind (manas) and is called "phenomena" (dharma).
Second, they shall be explained in relation to one another:
that which possesses substance and resistance is called "form" (rūpa).
Discussing this in general terms:
Sound, fragrance, flavor, and so forth are all characterized by substantial resistance;
yet such is the nature of the sensory object of form.
Because the characteristics of resistance and obstruction are prominent, it is specifically designated by that name.
Furthermore, shape and color are also termed "rūpa" (form).
Resonant tones are called "sound," and fragrant scents are called "incense";
these names are insufficient [to describe it].
Among these, there are also rancid, acrid, and foul odors;
it would be impossible to enumerate them all,
so for now I shall retain only the term "fragrance."
This is the gateway of inexhaustible discourse.
That which may be tasted and named is called "taste";
that which may be touched is called "contact."
The intrinsic nature is called "dharma"; the name is thus.
This is the second section.
To distinguish their essential natures:
the five faculties, beginning with the eye,
have pure matter as their essence.
According to the Abhidharma,
its substance consists of pure matter derived from the four great elements;
according to the *Tattvasiddhi*, however:
It has as its essence the provisional form (rūpa) composed of the four great elements (mahābhūta).
Question: Since the four great elements neither increase nor decrease, [how can there be such provisional forms?]
How is it that the five types of faculties are each distinct?
The explanation states:
it is the natural law (*dharmatā*) that they are composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Just as the four external great elements do not increase or decrease,
yet the rice, wheat, beans, and so forth produced by them each differ from one another;
likewise, due to karma, there arise differences among the sense faculties.
There is karma that can produce a single aggregate of the four great elements constituting the eye-faculty, which is able to see forms;
and so on, up to karma that produces a single aggregate of the four great elements constituting the body-faculty, which is able to perceive tangibles.
Just as by giving lamps one obtains the faculty of the eye,
and by giving bells, gongs, and so forth one obtains the faculty of the ear,
so it is in all such cases.
Question: If it is by means of karma that one is able to see and even to perceive, what is the use of the sense faculties?
Explanation:
Although karma serves as the cause,
it must necessarily rely upon sense faculties as conditions; just as grain, though obtained through karma, must necessarily rely upon seeds.
This is also the case here.
Next, the sense-base of mind (manāyatana) is distinguished;
it has the mind as its essence.
According to the Abhidharma,
all six consciousnesses that are capable of producing subsequent states are the mental faculty (manas); they are collectively designated as the sense-base of mind (manāyatana).
All other mental factors, such as perception, feeling, and formations,
which arise subsequently to the former,
are not the sense-base of mind (manāyatana).
Because it is subsumed within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). Question:
If all six consciousnesses that are capable of producing subsequent states are entirely the mind-faculty (*manas*), [how is this so]?
Is it that the six consciousnesses that arise are collectively designated as "mental consciousness"?
The treatise itself explains:
there are two kinds of bases.
First is the common support:
the six consciousnesses arise together, supported by the mental faculty (*manas*).
Second is the uncommon support.
The minds of the six consciousnesses each rely on their own respective sense organs;
when viewed in relation to their common support,
they are all collectively termed "mental consciousness."
In view of their not having a common basis,
the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and so forth,
each receive their own distinct name.
It is not termed "mental consciousness.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*,
there are three interpretations of its meaning.
To discuss them by way of their general characteristics:
all four types of consciousness arise one after another.
All these are the mental faculty (manas-indriya);
they are collectively termed the mental base (mana-āyatana) in the sense that they arise from what precedes them.
It is synonymous with "mental consciousness" (manovijñāna) and is subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana).
Second, it distinguishes [itself] from the five sensory consciousnesses.
Excluding the arising of the five consciousnesses,
all other consciousnesses, perceptions, feelings, and formations arise subsequently to the preceding ones.
All of these are the sphere of mind (manāyatana).
According to this single gateway,
it refers to the mind that has successively ceased prior to the five consciousnesses.
This is subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), not the sphere of mind (*manāyatana*).
The three pairs of specific names clarify the sphere of mind by means of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Among the four mental aggregates— consciousness, perception, feeling,
and formations— the specific portion consisting of the final part of the formations that gives rise to the mental consciousness is designated as the sense-base of mind (manāyatana);
all others are subsumed within the sense-base of phenomena (dharmāyatana).
What is taught in the Mahāyāna is the same as in the Abhidharma;
such is the case regarding the internal sense-bases.
Next, the external bases (āyatana) are distinguished.
The five objects, such as form and so forth, have form as their substance.
This is according to the Abhidharma.
The matter, sound, fragrance, and so forth, produced by the four great elements,
constitute the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).
According to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Chengshi lun):
The four great elements take form, odor, taste, and touch as their four objects.
When the four great elements strike one another, sound is produced.
Thus, these four objects are the causes of the four great elements.
Sound is a great fruit;
the five sense objects are likewise.
Next, the sphere of mental phenomena (dharmāyatana) is analyzed.
The sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana) is broad and pervasive;
with the exception of the aforementioned eleven [spheres], all other conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are entirely included within the sphere of phenomena.
The essential nature is thus.
In the third section,
its characteristics will next be analyzed.
The eye-base is twofold:
first, the fleshly; second, the celestial.
The fleshly is of two kinds.
First, the faculty of retribution;
second, the faculty of growth.
These include all visual faculties belonging to humans, ghosts, animals, and so forth.
That which arises from past causes is called a root of retribution (*vipākendriya*);
that which obtains the eye through present conditions such as food, drink,
and medicine is called nurtured (*aupacayika*).
Within the divine eye,
there are also two kinds: first,
the faculty of retribution (vipākendriya).
Second is the skillful means:
from the desire realm heavens up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven,
one attains the pure eye obtained as a result of karmic retribution.
This is its resultant faculty.
Relying upon the four dhyānas to cultivate and attain the divine eye is its means.
Question: The sūtras state that there are five eyes.
Why, then, are only two kinds mentioned here?
The commentary states:
The wisdom-eye (prajñā-cakṣus), the dharma-eye (dharma-cakṣus), and the buddha-eye (buddha-cakṣus) have wisdom as their essential nature.
It is not a physical sense faculty (rūpīndriya);
therefore, it is not discussed here.
The same applies to the eye-base (cakṣurāyatana).
Next, the ear-base (śrotra-āyatana) is explained;
it is the same as the eye-faculty (cakṣur-indriya). The nose, tongue, and body bases (ghrāṇa-, jihvā-, kāya-āyatana) are likewise.
There are also two kinds:
first, flesh; second, celestial.
Flesh is the same as described previously.
In the heavens, there exist only the faculties born of retribution,
but not those of application. Why is this so?
The various devas of the desire realm [possess these] for the purpose of smelling fragrances, tasting flavors, and experiencing tactile sensations,
as well as for the adornment of their bodies.
Therefore, there are faculties that are results of maturation;
for the various devas of the form realm [possess them] in order to adorn their bodies.
There are also faculties that are results of maturation (vipākaja). However, the faculties of nose, tongue, and body are not of the nature of supernormal powers (abhijñā);
they perceive their objects only when those objects reach them.
Because one cannot know it through profound insight,
one does not rely on the skillful means of dhyāna to cultivate its arising.
[The interlocutor] asks:
If deities possess the nose, tongue, and body,
why are they not mentioned in the sūtras and śāstras? To explain:
The sūtras and śāstras state in truth that the deities above possess the faculties of nose, tongue, and body;
however, these three faculties do not possess the nature of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and are no different from those of humans.
Therefore, in the sūtras and śāstras,
the supernormal powers of the divine nose, the divine tongue, and so forth are not mentioned.
Next, the sense-base of the mind (manāyatana) is explained.
In the Abhidharma system,
immediately after the six consciousnesses arise,
they become the six mental faculties (manas).
In the *Tattvasiddhi*, the mental faculty (*manas*) has both general and specific aspects;
it refers to the mind at the final stage of the formations (*saṃskāra*).
Those who understand the mental consciousness distinguish it from all four types of minds.
That which arises subsequently is the mental faculty (*manas*).
Taking this as the general [definition],
there are three distinct meanings for its specific designation.
The final mind that follows the five consciousnesses and gives rise to the mental consciousness is, in some cases,
designated as the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*).
The final mind that follows after the two types of fivefold consciousnesses and gives rise to mental consciousness is called the sense-base of mind (manāyatana).
Third, the mind that arises following the sixth independent consciousness at the end of its activity is called the sense-base of mind (manāyatana).
If there is a mental consciousness that arises depending on the guidance of the preceding five consciousnesses,
it is called "fivefold consciousness" (pañcavijñāna).
That which arises without depending on the guidance of the five consciousnesses is termed "independent" (svatantra).
The specific names are thus.

Within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), the six consciousnesses are distinguished;
