According to that school, there are six consciousnesses.
Because they are subsumed within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), the meaning of the twelve spheres (*dvādaśāyatana*) has been briefly explained in this manner.

87. The Meaning of the Eighteen Dhātus (Part 8): An Elevenfold Analytical Explanation of the Meaning of the Eighteen Dhātus. 1. Analysis by way of the Three Aggregates; 2. Analysis by way of Internal and External; 3. Analysis by way of the Three Natures; 4. Analysis by way of the Grounds; 5. Analysis by way of Conditioned and Unconditioned; 6. Analysis by way of Tainted and Untainted; 7. Analysis by way of Learners and so forth; 8. Analysis by way of the Three Abandonments; 9. Analysis by way of the Three Pairs; 10. Analysis by way of the Different Objects of Consciousness; 11. First, the Explanation of Names.
The six faculties, such as the eye, the six objects, such as form, and the six consciousnesses constitute these eighteen [elements].
That which is capable of producing [a result] is called a faculty (*indriya*).
Because they can give rise to consciousness,
they are called "objects" (*viṣaya*); because they defile, they are called "dust," for they sully the mind.
However, these [objects] such as form (rūpa) are designated by their respective names and termed the "six objects" (viṣaya);
yet they are also called "dust" (rajas).
This name is established specifically in contrast to the defiled mind.
This is because the pure mind arises predominantly by taking principle as its object.
Since they arise based on the objective entities that serve as the support for defilement, they are specifically designated as "objects" (*viṣaya*) in contrast to defilement.
That which is capable of cognizing is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
Because they exhaust all sense objects,
these eighteen are called "elements" (dhātu) in the sutras.
It is also called "nature" (dhātu).
The differentiation of realms is termed "realm" (dhātu);
the differentiation of natures is termed "nature" (dhātu).
Because the natures of all phenomena are distinct, they are called "elements" (*dhātu*). This concludes the first section.
Next, the various elements are analyzed according to the three categories (*tri-rāśi*).
Regarding these three categories:
That which is called "neither matter nor mind" refers to the eighteen elements (*dhātus*). Among these,
the five sense organs and the five sense objects are exclusively matter.
The mind-faculty and the six consciousnesses are exclusively mind.
Within the dharma-realm,
the three aggregates are fully contained.
According to the Abhidharma,
non-manifesting (avijñapti) wholesome and unwholesome [karma] is classified as matter (rūpa-dharma), while perception (saṃjñā),
feeling (vedanā), mental formations (saṃskāra), and so forth, are classified as mind (citta-dharma).
The remaining fourteen non-associated formations and the three unconditioned phenomena are neither matter nor mind;
this is established in the *Tattvasiddhi* (Chengshi lun).
Past and future objects of the five sense-fields, the four great elements,
and other forms are considered the dharma of form (*rūpadharma*).
[This includes] the mind that has successively ceased prior to the five consciousnesses.
These are mental phenomena (citta-dharma),
provisionally designated as sentient beings, wholesome and unwholesome, non-informative action (avijñapti), and the three unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta);
they are neither form nor mind.
The three aggregates are thus.
Within the category of form (*rūpa*), they are further analyzed through three distinct gateways.
First, all forms are analyzed with respect to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*,
visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility are the causes of the four great elements and are able to constitute them.
It does not constitute a great accomplishment.
The single category of the auditory object (śabda-viṣaya) is the fruit of the four great elements (mahābhūta).
It arises based on the four great elements,
yet it does not grasp the great elements as a whole.
The five faculties, such as the eye, are formed by the four great elements.
Regarding the nature of form within the dharma-realm,
its meaning is not fixed.
If one discusses the form-dharmas of the five sense objects belonging to the past and future, [they are non-existent].
The same applies to the five sense objects (*viṣaya*);
they do not constitute a great accomplishment.
This also holds for the past and future five sense faculties (*indriya*).
The same applies to the five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*);
they are composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). Other external derivative forms (*upādāyarūpa*) are likewise composed of the four great elements.
When the four great elements are viewed in relation to one another,
there exists the principle that they can give rise to one another and accomplish one another even in the absence of mutual characteristics.
In the Abhidharma system,
the five sense organs such as the eye, as well as the objects of form, sound, odor, taste, and the forms within the sphere of mental phenomena (dharmāyatana),
are all derived from the four great elements.
The element of tangibility is indeterminate;
the seven kinds, such as lightness and so forth,
are derived from the four great elements.
Hardness, moisture, warmth,
and motion are the tactile qualities of the four great elements; they are not themselves created by the four great elements.
Question: Do the four great elements collectively create all material forms, or do they create them individually?
On this point, the commentators differ.
Some proclaim that a single set of the four great elements constitutes all derived forms. Others, moreover, say:
Those who gather act together;
those who differ act separately;
these are the various mental factors that remain.
The four great elements are produced separately;
there is no principle of their being combined.
Second, they are distinguished according to their opposition.
Form is of three kinds:
first, visible and resistant;
second, invisible and resistant.
Three are invisible and non-obstructive;
one type in the form realm is visible and obstructive.
That which is the range of the eye is called "visible.
Because it is an obstacle and is confronted by the physical sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*), it is called "possessing resistance" (*sapratigha*).
This applies likewise to sound, odor, taste, and touch.
This is "invisible and resistant.
It is called "invisible" because it is not within the range of the eye;
"resistant" is as explained previously.
The five faculties beginning with the eye, as well as non-informative matter (avijñapti-rūpa),
are invisible and non-obstructive;
they are not within the range of the visual faculty.
Therefore, it is invisible;
it is the object-condition for the mind,
but it is not confronted by the obstructive sense faculties of form.
Therefore, it is called "non-obstructive" (apratigha).
Third, there is the classification according to sensation (vedanā):
if a material phenomenon (rūpa-dharma) can cause a conscious perception (buddhi-citta) through its destruction or oppression.
To give rise to it is called "receiving";
not to give rise to the thought of awareness is called "not receiving."
As stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*:
"If the five faculties,
such as the eye, are present..."
That which can give rise to the mind of feeling is called "feeling" (vedanā).
If it exists in the past or future, it does not give rise to the mind of cognition.
This is called non-acceptance.
Form, fragrance, taste,
and touch exist in the present.
That which is not separated from the sense faculties is called "feeling" (vedanā);
that which is otherwise is "non-feeling."
Regarding the sense-object of sound and the form within the sense-object of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*),
one does not accept them at all,
because no cognition arises toward them.
The nature of material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) is thus.
Next, the mental phenomena (*cittadharma*) are analyzed;
therein, they are distinguished according to applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
According to the Abhidharma,
within the five consciousnesses,
vitarka and vicāra are necessarily present.
The mind-faculty (manas), mental consciousness (manovijñāna),
and the dharma-element (dharmadhātu) are three distinct categories in meaning up to and including the first dhyāna.
In the dhyāna of concentration, there is both vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought). In the intermediate dhyāna stage, there is no vitarka, but there is vicāra.
From the second dhyāna upward, there is certainly no vitarka or vicāra.
Question: [Why is this?]
Why are the five consciousnesses not like this?
The explanation says:
the five consciousnesses exist only within the desire realm and the first dhyāna.
In the higher stages, however, they do not exist.
Therefore, the five consciousnesses occur only with vitarka and vicāra.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*, however:
Within the five consciousnesses, there is definitely no vitarka (applied thought) or vicāra (sustained thought),
because there is no mental deliberation within the five consciousnesses.
The mental faculty (*manas*), the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the mental element (*dharmadhātu*) are roughly the same as in the Abhidharma.
The details differ.
That school proclaims that vitarka and vicāra exist within a single moment of mind.
It pervades all three realms,
because it is the coarse and subtle characteristic of this mind;
thus, within the three realms:
The minds of the stages of the desire realm necessarily possess vitarka and vicāra;
[this is likewise true for] the form and formless realms.
The expedient means of dhyāna exist,
but the substance of concentration does not,
because it is quiescent.
The mental phenomena (*cittadharma*) are thus.
Next, the phenomena that are neither form nor mind (*na-rūpa-na-citta-dharma*) are distinguished;
therein, they are analyzed according to their existence and non-existence.
If one considers the principle of emptiness,
the entire dharma-realm is designated as "existent.
Thus, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
The conditioned and the unconditioned are called "existence.
They are devoid of self and what belongs to a self.
It is named "non-existence" (abhāva).
It is distinguished according to its characteristics into three unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛtadharma).
This is a non-existent dharma that is neither form nor mind;
its existence is indeterminate.
This is what is proclaimed in the Abhidharma teachings.
The *Tattvasiddhi* proclaims that the fourteen dissociated formations (*viprayuktasamskāra*) are dharmas that are neither form (*rūpa*) nor mind (*citta*).
The provisional designation of sentient beings as having neither wholesome nor unwholesome non-action—
considering these as dharmas that are neither form nor mind— concludes these two gates.
Next, one proceeds to distinguish the various elements (*dhātu*) by way of the internal and external.
Within this, if one discusses it according to the threefold division,
the six sense organs are internal and the six sense objects are external.
The six consciousnesses constitute the middle.
Analyzing them into two parts,
the faculties and objects are as described above.
The six consciousnesses are indeterminate;
in the Abhidharma system,
they are subsumed as internal.
Therefore, that treatise states:
"The internal elements are said to be twelve;
in the *Tattvasiddhi*, it is not so."
According to that school, the six consciousnesses are subsumed under the *dharmāyatana* (the sphere of mental objects).
Thus, the six consciousnesses are categorized as being external [to the internal sense bases]. This concludes the three gates.
Next, the various elements (dhātus) are analyzed according to the three natures.
Wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate are these three natures.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*,
the five sense organs, the five objects, and the five consciousnesses are invariably indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
The mental faculty (manas), mental consciousness (manovijñāna), and the dharma-element (dharmadhātu) encompass all three natures.
In the Abhidharma system, [this is so].
The five faculties beginning with the eye, as well as the objects of smell, taste, and touch,
are invariably indeterminate (avyākṛta).
The remainder may belong to all three natures.
Therefore, that treatise states:
"The indeterminate consists of eight types;
the remainder are either wholesome or unwholesome."
The mental faculty (*manas*), the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) can be known as either wholesome or unwholesome.
As for the meaning of the wholesomeness and unwholesomeness of the five consciousnesses— form, sound, and so forth—
it is according to that school’s tenet as follows:
Wholesome mental states such as prostration and praise constitute wholesome form and sound;
unwholesome mental states give rise to the two types of karma of body and speech.
These are unwholesome forms and sounds.
When the five consciousnesses arise in their respective stages by taking wholesome objects as conditions,
they are judged to be wholesome.
If the five consciousnesses arise by taking as their objects things that are subject to greed, anger, and so forth,
they are judged to be unwholesome.
A question is asked:
Why is it that in the Abhidharma (Vibhāṣā) system, form and sound are declared to encompass all three natures (tridharmas),
whereas in the Satyasiddhiśāstra, they are said to be only indeterminate (avyākṛta)? The explanation is as follows:
In the Abhidharma, the two types of karma— bodily and vocal—
are of the nature of form (rūpa) and sound (śabda);
therefore, they pertain to all three moral natures.
In the *Tattvasiddhi*, all that is good and evil exists within the conventional;
in the ultimate, there is none.
However, in that treatise,
the five sense objects are exclusively real and do not extend to conventional designations; therefore,
they possess neither goodness nor evil.
Question: For what reason do goodness and evil exist only within the conventional (prajñapti) and not apply to real dharmas (dharmatā)?
Explanation:
In that school’s view, benefit and harm exist only within the continuity [of the mind];
they do not exist in a single moment because [the moment] lacks duration.
Furthermore, it is asked: "In the Abhidharma-dharmaskandha-śāstra, it is taught that the five consciousnesses pertain to all three natures (trividha).
Why, then, does the *Tattvasiddhi* state that they are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
The explanation says:
The Abhidharma does not establish the doctrine of the provisional;
it proclaims that both good and evil exist entirely within the real.
Therefore, within a single moment of the five sensory consciousnesses—
Good and evil exist; in the *Tattvasiddhi*,
good and evil exist only within the conventional (prajñapti),
whereas the five consciousnesses are exclusively real.
Therefore, there is neither good nor evil.
Furthermore, according to the Abhidharma,
mental factors arise simultaneously with the mind.
Within the sphere of the five consciousnesses,
there exist categories of good and evil; these are determined by the primary mind (the *manas*) following their numerical count.
Therefore, it is said that good and evil [arise] within the *Tattvasiddhi* (Satyasiddhi) system; therein,
the mind alone does not function simultaneously.
The five consciousnesses arise to directly perceive the five sense objects;
there is no further meaning beyond this,
and thus they possess neither goodness nor evil.
Question: If, within the category of truly established phenomena (*dravyasat*), the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and lack both good and evil,
then the mind of the five consciousnesses should not constitute wholesome conduct (*sucarita*).
The commentary states:
According to that school, the essential nature of the five consciousnesses is not,
in reality, a sublime action (sucarita).
There is no fault in the subsequent mental activity following the five consciousnesses;
this is precisely what is called "sublime conduct" (sucarita) according to the Mahāyāna teachings.
Ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles are the same as in the Abhidharma.
In the realm of the true retribution of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
the faculties and consciousnesses are exclusively wholesome.
The dust [of sensory objects] penetrates all three natures; this concludes the four gates.
Next, there is a distinction between one's own stage and other stages.
Regarding "one's own stage":
Dwelling in the desire realm,
within its own level, there are the faculties,
objects, and consciousnesses.
Possessing all [perfections],
his body is in the first dhyāna,
within its own stage.
The six sense faculties are fully present;
there are only four objects:
visible forms, sounds, tangibles, and mental phenomena.
Since they lack solid food,
they have no odors or tastes.
Consciousness likewise has four types.
Excluding nose-consciousness and tongue-consciousness,
because there is no odor or flavor [in those realms].
When the body is in the second dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna...
Within its own stage,
the six faculties and four objects are the same as those of the first dhyāna;
however, consciousness is not fixed.
In the Abhidharma system,
there is only the mental consciousness;
all other consciousnesses are absent.
If there were no other consciousnesses,
how could one perceive forms, hear sounds, or experience tangibles?
That treatise explains as follows:
From the second dhyāna upward, one borrows the consciousness of the first dhyāna;
therefore, one is able to see forms, hear sounds, and perceive tangibles.
The *Tattvasiddhi* states that these are identical to those of the first dhyāna.
That location possesses the four types of consciousness— eye, ear, body, and mind. Therefore,
while the body resides within the four formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*),
its specific status is not fixed.
In the Hīnayāna teachings,
there are only the mental faculty (*manas*), the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*),
and the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*). In the Mahāyāna, it is taught that these faculties, objects, and consciousnesses are identical to the four dhyānas.
The Mahāyāna teaches that they still possess form;
therefore, it is thus for their own stage.
As for what is called "another stage":
The faculties of the nose, tongue, and body, as well as their respective consciousnesses,
arise only in their own respective stages and do not extend to other stages.
This applies to the faculties of the eye, ear, and mind, as well as these respective consciousnesses.
With the body on a lower level,
in whatever place within a higher level there may be.
All of them are able to arise.
Among the six sense objects, odors, tastes,
and tangibles are perceived only by the faculties and consciousnesses of their own respective stages.
They do not extend to other stages,
because there is no profound knowledge [of them].
This refers to the element of form and the element of sound.
In the teachings of the Hīnayāna,
from the fourth dhyāna downwards,
[the mind] follows the body wherever it may be.
Within other realms,
these are all seen and heard; however,
they do not extend to the formless realm.
That which is taught in the Mahāyāna up to the Form Realm (rūpadhātu) is the same as that of the Hīnayāna.
Within the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu),
there are both similarities and differences;
these refer to ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) and those of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha).
In the formless realm,
all forms and sounds belonging to other stages are neither seen nor heard.
Because their minds are weak and inferior,
this is the same as the Hīnayāna;
the bodhisattva remains therein.
Within other lands,
all forms and sounds are seen and heard.
Because of mastery over the mind and because the faculties are keen and sharp;
this differs from the Hīnayāna.
The dharma-realm is not fixed;
according to the Abhidharma,
it is the realm of tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharmadhātu*).
From the fourth dhyāna downwards,
wherever the body may be located,
it pertains to other stages (bhūmi).
All are able to know through conditions;
however, when birth and abiding occur within the formless realm, it is not thus.
They take as their objects only the dharmas of their own level and of higher levels,
but not those of lower levels;
therefore, that treatise states:
The formless [realms] do not take the contaminated phenomena of lower levels as their object;
the uncontaminated dharma-realm (anāsrava-dharmadhātu), however, is not like this.
Within other stages, wherever the body may be,
one is able to take them as objects of knowledge through cognition.
Without distinguishing between superior and inferior levels,
if one follows the *Tattvasiddhi*,
all outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) and outflow-free (*anāsrava*) states of other stages [are included].
Within the three realms,
wherever the body may be,
one is able to know through mental objects.
However, in that treatise it is stated that although those in the formless realm take as their object the contaminated phenomena of the lower stages, [they do not produce afflictions].
The mind is not at ease,
like burning tendons or feathers;
it is not that there is no object of perception.
In the Mahāyāna teachings,
it is the same as in the *Tattvasiddhi*.
A question is asked:
If there is a person whose body is in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) who, using the eye of the first dhyāna,
sees forms of their own level as well as forms of other levels,
by which level is the visual consciousness produced therein subsumed?
The commentary states:
It is subsumed under the stage of the first dhyāna where it arises,
because it arises in dependence upon the eye.
He asked again:
"Suppose there is a person whose body is in the realm of desire (kāmadhātu) or the stage of the first dhyāna, yet they employ the eye of the second dhyāna,
and so on, up to employing the eye of the fourth dhyāna stage."
When one sees forms of one's own stage as well as forms of other stages,
by what stage is the eye-consciousness thus produced subsumed?
According to the Abhidharma:
All [these] are subsumed under the first dhyāna.
Within that school’s system, from the second dhyāna upward,
there is no visual consciousness whatsoever.
Regarding the statement "borrowing the consciousness of the first dhyāna" because it discerns all forms:
this means that from the second dhyāna upward, the eye-consciousness is identical to the consciousness of the first dhyāna.
Because they are similar in their coarseness and subtlety,
it is said that [the latter] "borrows" from the former; it is not that it borrows from what is spoken by another.
There are persons born in the second dhyāna or above who,
using the eyes of their own level as well as those of other levels,
perceive both the forms of their own level and the forms of other levels.
One should know that the eye-consciousness thus produced is likewise subsumed under the first dhyāna;
the same may be understood for the subsequent stages by analogy.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*,
all visual consciousness is designated according to the locus of the eye.
It does not depend on a lower consciousness;
in the Mahāyāna teachings,
there is no fixed determination in the texts.

For the most part, this is consistent with the *Tattvasiddhi*, as there is no need for a borrowed consciousness (*upādāna-vijñāna*). Since this is the case for visual consciousness, so it is for the others.
The ear-consciousness is the same as this.
As for the body-consciousness,
it extends from the First Dhyāna downwards.
It is said therein: "In the second dhyāna and above,
it is the touch that is perceived."
It must be in that very place.
The consciousness produced there is also comprised within the first dhyāna. This concludes the five doors.
Next, regarding the distinction between the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*):
within the teachings of the Hīnayāna, the first seventeen [categories] are exclusively conditioned.
The dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) encompasses both the conditioned (saṃskṛta) and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
Form-dharmas (rūpadharma), mind-dharmas (cittadharma), and non-form/non-mind dharmas (arūpa-acittadharma) constitute the conditioned.
Space, cessation through deliberation, and cessation not through deliberation—
these are its unconditioned [dharmas] within the Mahāyāna teachings.
The essence of the true sense-consciousnesses of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
their functioning is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Among the six sense-objects:
The three unconditioned phenomena are exclusively unconditioned;
all others are [conditioned].
Speaking from the perspective of the actual recompense of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, this is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
the others are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). This concludes the six gates.
Next, regarding the distinction between the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*):
within the Abhidharma system, the five faculties, the five objects, and the five consciousnesses are exclusively contaminated.
Because they arise from the outflows (*āsrava*), because the outflows depend upon them for their abiding,
[these are] the faculty of mind (*manas*), mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
Regarding the permeable (*sāsrava*) and the non-permeable (*anāsrava*): in the *Tattvasiddhi*, it is stated that if one cuts off the outflows (*āsrava*), [the result is the non-permeable].
It is called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*).
This is the same as the Abhidharma.
If that which does not produce outflows is named "outflow-free," then...
The realms of ordinary beings are invariably with outflows; the realms of those beyond training are invariably without outflows.
For the practitioner who is not yet fixed,
all places where fetters have been severed are entirely untainted (*anāsrava*).
In the Mahāyāna Dharma, all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*) are points where the fetters (*saṃyojana*) have not yet been severed.
The fundamental substance of the faculties and consciousnesses of the true recompense of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is untainted (anāsrava);
their manifest clarity appears as tainted (sāsrava).
Among the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*),
they are both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). As for the five sense objects, such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth:
Speaking in terms of the actual retribution of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
that is untainted (anāsrava),
while the rest is tainted (sāsrava).
Among the objects of the mental faculty (dharmāyatana),
the analytical cessations (pratisaṃkhyānirodha) and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) are exclusively untainted (anāsrava).
The remainder is as in the case of the five sense objects; this concludes the seven gates.
Next, the various elements (dhātus) are distinguished according to the categories of those in training (śaikṣa) and so forth.
There are three kinds of phenomena (dharma).
First is the dharma of those in training (*śaikṣadharma*),
which refers to the untainted causes (*anāsravahetu*) of those belonging to the three vehicles.
Second is the dharma of those beyond training (*aśaikṣadharma*).
This refers to the untainted fruits of the three vehicles.
The "neither-learner-nor-non-learner" category refers to all other tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) as well as the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
The study of these is likewise.
Within the Dharma of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna),
there are the mental faculty (manas), the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), and the dharma-element (dharmadhātu).
The meaning applies to three types:
the cause of the untainted,
as well as the vision of those in training and so forth.
This is called "training.
When a person in training wanders through contemplation yet has not yet severed the outflows or the fetters,
this is termed "the right view of one in training" (śaikṣa-samyagdṛṣṭi).
Those who possess the supreme fruit of the untainted and the wisdom of the vision of those beyond training (aśaikṣa) are called "beyond training.
What is this supreme fruit of the untainted?
These are what are called the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
What is the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi*)?
It refers to the untainted contemplation (*anāsravamanasikāra*) of a person beyond training.
The remaining mental faculty (*manas*), mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*),
and the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) are said to be neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
As for the other fifteen elements:
They are exclusively neither-learner-nor-non-learner,
as distinguished in the Mahāyāna.
The eighteen elements (dhātu) of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles are the same as those in the Hīnayāna.
The eighteen realms (*dhātu*) of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are all encompassed by these three types. These include the faculties,
objects, and consciousnesses of the actual retribution realm (*vipākabhūmi*) of all Bodhisattvas.
All are termed "those in training" (*śaikṣa*).
As stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*:
"The bodhisattva of the lineage possesses the excellence of the six sense bases (*ṣadāyatana-viśeṣa*)."
This is the natural law from beginningless time;
it is obtained as such through the cultivation of virtue since the past.
All these are the six faculties of training;
based upon them, the mind arises,
which constitutes the six consciousnesses of training.
The realm of the pure land attained through actual retribution,
as well as the realms manifested based on samādhi—
these are the six sense objects of training.
The realms of actual retribution, the sense organs, objects, and consciousnesses of all Tathāgatas constitute their state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
All others are neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*). These eight categories are concluded.
Next, the various realms are distinguished according to the three types of abandonment.
Regarding these three types of abandonment: the first is that which is abandoned through vision (*darśana-heya*).
The second is abandonment through cultivation;
the third is non-abandonment.
Dharmas abandoned by seeing the truths are termed "abandoned by seeing."
The dharmas abandoned through the path of cultivation are called "abandoned by cultivation.
All other dharmas, such as the untainted (anāsrava) and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), are called "not to be abandoned.
This is according to the Abhidharma.
The five faculties, the five objects, and the five consciousnesses—
these fifteen elements (*dhātu*) are abandoned only through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
As for the remaining three elements:
It is both abandoned through the vision of the truths,
abandoned through the path of cultivation, and also not abandoned.
That which is associated with the delusions of view is said to be abandoned by seeing;
that which is associated with the delusions of cultivation...
These are said to be abandoned through cultivation;
the remainder are called unabandoned.
This is according to the *Tattvasiddhi*.

The five faculties, the five objects, and the five consciousnesses are all subject to abandonment through the vision of the truths (darśana-heya) as well as abandonment through the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-heya);
they are not subject to non-abandonment.
Because they sever the delusions of views,
they cause the three miserable realms, the five sense organs, the five sense objects, and the five consciousnesses not to arise; therefore,
they are judged as being severed by insight (*darśana-heya*).
Because they are abandoned through cultivation,
they cause the five faculties, five objects, and five consciousnesses of those humans and devas not to arise;
thus, they are classified as being abandoned by cultivation.
Therefore, that treatise states:
"Dharmas abandoned through vision" refers to the conceit of self-identity (*asmimāna*) characterized by manifesting signs, as well as all other dharmas arising from it.
Regarding the dharmas to be abandoned through cultivation:
they do not manifest the conceit of signs nor the other various dharmas arising therefrom; such is the essential nature of the delusions abandoned through seeing the truths.
This is the conceit of manifesting signs;
the karmic retribution arising therefrom constitutes the remaining dharmas.
The essence of the afflictions abandoned through the path of cultivation does not manifest the signs; the karma and its results produced by pride constitute these other dharmas.
In that *Tattvasiddhi*, it states:
"The severance of cause and effect is termed analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)."
Therefore, the two kinds of afflictions— the results of seeing and cultivation—
are designated as being abandoned through seeing and abandoned through the path of cultivation, respectively, according to their roots.
The mind-faculty (*manas*), mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) are the same as in the Abhidharma;
such are the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*) in the Mahāyāna teachings.
All are comprised within three types.
All dharmas of the eighteen realms of birth and death that are eliminated upon the first stage are termed "abandoned by insight."
All eighteen dharmas of the realms that are eliminated from the second bhūmi upward are abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya). However,
the faculties and consciousnesses formed by the actual retribution of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are uninterrupted.
The "dust" (rajas) is categorized into three types; this concludes the nine gates.
Next, the various realms (dhātu) are analyzed according to three pairs.
As for these three pairs:
As stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*:
first, resistance regarding the object (*ālambana-pratighāta*);
second, resistance regarding obstruction (*āvaraṇa-pratighāta*).
There are three kinds of resistance (*pratigha*). Regarding resistance with respect to objects (*ālambana-pratigha*):
it refers to all material sense faculties (*rūpīndriya*) as well as the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
That which is capable of encountering external objects through the faculty of cognition is called "having resistance with respect to objects" (*viṣayapratighāta*).
Within this category, there are the six faculties,
the six consciousnesses, and the mental factor-element (*dharmadhātu*).
These are the objects with resistance (*sapratigha*):
the five sense-objects such as form (*rūpa*), etc., and those non-mental phenomena within the dharma-sphere (*dharmadhātu*).
These are the objects without resistance (*apratigha*).
Because they are non-sentient.
Regarding "obstructive resistance":
it refers to the mutual obstruction and opposition between the material sense faculties and their corresponding material objects.
That which is obstructed and does not pass through is called "obstructive resistance" (*pratigha*).
Within this category, ten elements are obstructive, namely:
the five faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body, and the five objects of form and so forth.
The remaining seven mind-elements and the mental-object-element are entirely without resistance (*apratigha*),
because they are not material forms that obstruct one another.
Question: If the five sense organs and the five sense objects were obstructive, then forms, odors, tastes,
and so forth should not be perceived within the locations of the sense organs, such as the eyes.
If they were to possess [space], they would not constitute an obstruction.
The treatise states:
"Because they each abide within an accumulation of atoms (paramāṇu-saṃcaya), they are still termed obstructions."

Regarding "having resistance as its object" (*sappatighālambana*): mental states such as consciousness and mental factors are called "having resistance as their object" because they are able to take objects as their cognitive focus.
Within this category,
a portion of seven elements is characterized by resistance.
This refers to the seven mind-elements (*cittadhātu*) and a portion of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*).
The remainder are non-resistant (*apratigha*), because they lack an object of cognition (*ālambana*). This concludes the ten gates.
Next, the differences in conditions regarding the various consciousnesses are clarified as explained in the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*:
"In the realm of form, two consciousnesses cognize [it]."
The same applies up to the element of tangibility.
All other thirteen elements are exclusively objects of the mental consciousness.
This explains that the five objects, such as form and so forth,
should be divided into the respective objects of the five consciousnesses.
Because the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) universally takes all phenomena as its objects,
it can also take these as its objects;
this is not the case for the remaining six sense organs, the six consciousnesses, or the phenomena that serve as their objects.
The five consciousnesses do not discern [objects]; only the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) takes them as its object.
In the *Tattvasiddhi*, there is no definitive judgment in the text [regarding this].
There are differing explanations of this term.
Some explain it as being the same as the Abhidharma.
Others further say:
"The six sense organs, the six consciousnesses, and the mental objects (dharmas) are the same as in the Abhidharma;
they are perceived exclusively by the mental consciousness."
The five objects, such as visible form and so forth,
are perceived only by the five consciousnesses;
the mental consciousness does not perceive them.
If it were the mental consciousness that perceives objects,
then the blind should see forms and the deaf should hear sounds.
One should know the hardness or softness of objects that are not touched;
all such cases are to be understood in this way.
Because those who are blind, deaf, and so forth do not see or hear,
it is clear that the mind does not take them as objects.
This is stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
This is explained in the same way as the subsequent commentary.
According to the actual treatise,
the mental consciousness universally takes all five sense objects as its conditions.
However, they are not differentiated. How is this known?
It is like a person in the present who perceives all forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles throughout the ten directions.
Although it is known that [the mental consciousness] takes all as its objects, it does not clearly perceive color, fragrance, taste, and so forth,
because these are not the primary objects of the mind.
Therefore, it is not understood. If [the mind] were able to perceive all objects universally,
why did Nāgārjuna proclaim that the mental consciousness does not know the five sensory objects?
The commentary states:
Nāgārjuna says that what is "not known" is not as clearly manifest as that which is known by the five consciousnesses.
Therefore, it is said that one does not know;
this does not mean that there is no objective condition at all regarding the meaning of the eighteen realms.
This is a brief summary. 88.
The Meaning of the Twenty-five Existences (End of Section 8). Regarding the meaning of the twenty-five existences: there are twenty-five existences.
This is set forth in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Because there is an effect arising from a cause, it is called "existence" (bhava).
Existence is differentiated and distinct,
comprising twenty-five types.
What are they? As stated in the sūtras,
there are fourteen [realms] in the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
That which is called hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, and asuras constitutes four;
together with the humans of the four continents, they form five.
These are further divided into four,
which together with the previous ones make eight;
the six heavens of the desire realm are further divided into six.
Including the previous fourteen,
there are seven in the form realm;
together with the former, they constitute twenty-one existences in total.
Those four dhyāna stages constitute four [abodes];
the Brahmā King of the Intermediate Realm constitutes the fifth;
and the realm of the Non-conceptual Devas constitutes the sixth.
All the Śuddhāvāsa heavens combined constitute the seventh [category].
There are four formless realms, namely the four spheres of emptiness; these, when added to the preceding, total twenty-five.
Question: For what reason are the inhabitants of the four continents divided into four types,
whereas the five Pure Abodes and others are combined into one?
The commentary states:
Separation and combination each follow what is appropriate.
For now, based on one gate, they are divided in this manner.
The twenty-five states of existence have been briefly distinguished. 89.
The Meaning of the Forty Abodes (End of Section 8): Regarding the "meaning of the forty abodes," as for what is called "abiding":
The dwelling places where sentient beings of the three realms reside are called "abodes.
These abodes differ from one another and are divided into forty types.
Within that, the desire realm consists of twenty locations;
the eight great hells constitute eight of these.
Animals and hungry ghosts are further divided into two;
together with the preceding [eight], they constitute ten.
The inhabitants of the four continents together with those of the six heavens of the desire realm constitute ten;
added to the previous [ten], they total twenty.
Within the stages of the form realm (rūpadhātu), there are sixteen [levels].
In the first dhyāna, there are two:
namely, the Brahmakāyika heaven and the Brahmapurohita heaven.
In the stage of the first dhyāna there is the Great Brahmā King;
why is he not mentioned?
Because he dwells in the same location as the Brahmā-purohita devas.
Therefore, they are not discussed separately.
The second dhyāna has three [levels], namely:
the Heaven of Limited Light (Parīttābha), the Heaven of Immeasurable Light (Apramāṇābha), and the Heaven of Radiant Sound (Ābhāsvara).
Including the previous [two], there are five in total.
Within the third dhyāna, there are three:
namely, the Heaven of Limited Purity (Parīttaśubha), the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity (Apramāṇaśubha), and the Heaven of Universal Purity (Śubhakṛtsna).
Including the preceding ones, there are eight.
Within the stages of the four dhyānas, they should be divided into three:
namely, the Heaven of Merit-Love (Puṇyaprasava), the Heaven of Merit-Birth (Anabhraka), and the Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala).
Including the previous eleven,
and adding the five types of *anāgāmin*, there are sixteen in total.
The *asaṃjñisattva* (non-percipient beings) share the same location as the *bṛhatphala* (vast fruit) gods.
Therefore, they are not explained separately.
By means of these sixteen,
combined with the preceding ones, they constitute thirty-six locations in total.
The four formless heavens,
added to the preceding forty,
constitute the total when considering the realm of form.
If one separately distinguishes the Mahābrahmā heaven and the Unconscious Heaven (asaṃjñisattva),
then there are forty-two abodes.
The dwelling [of the practitioner] is thus.
This concludes the end of the eighth fascicle of the *Dacheng yi zhang* (Treatise on the Meaning of the Mahāyāna).
